case_study_insert.main_stem: Quillstone Low-Carbon Concrete (QLC) is a public limited company in the low-carbon construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 75. Founded in 2007 by Elena Quill, it supplies ready-mixed concrete to contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. QLC plans to invest $1,050,000 in a new batching plant using recycled aggregate and a geopolymer binder, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and a $650,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $21.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. QLC faces two problems: failed batches run at 2.2% and offcut waste from the conventional line is 4.5%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log, Q2 2025: the pilot batching line produced 18,000 cubic metres with a failed-batch rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about strength variation fell from 31 to 16 per month. Average delivery is 4 days. A survey of 500 contractors found that 57% would specify low-carbon concrete and 49% accept a price premium of $0.80 per cubic metre. Offcut waste is 4.5% on the conventional line against 2.1% on the pilot. Records show 18 of 75 plant staff are certified on the geopolymer mixer; courses cost $820 each.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Quillstone Low-Carbon Concrete for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, lifting borrowing costs. (2) The minimum wage rose 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.50 an hour from April 2026. (3) Recycled aggregate and cement input costs increased 10.2% year-on-year while construction inflation is 5.8% and infrastructure output grew 3.2%.

questions.question_text: QLC raised $650,000 through a share issue to fund its $1,050,000 batching plant. Explain two advantages for QLC of a share issue over a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings $650,000 with no interest or capital repayment, so QLC can commit the money to the geopolymer batching plant while already bearing fixed costs of $450,000 a year and a $400,000 bank loan. Unlike debt, dividends are payable only if profits allow, which suits a business whose 2.2% failed-batch rate may take time to fall.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral or place the $1,050,000 plant at risk of repossession if infrastructure demand slips, and it strengthens the balance sheet for future borrowing. As a public limited company QLC can also use the issue to widen its shareholder base, giving access to further capital for the 4-day delivery operation and helping absorb the 10.2% rise in recycled aggregate and cement costs without increasing its loan burden.

The $650,000 also reduces reliance on the $400,000 bank loan, leaving more of the $450,000 fixed-cost budget available to bring the 2.2% failed-batch rate down as the new plant beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to QLC's share issue, loan and costs.

questions.question_text: QLC is launching its low-carbon concrete. Consider national television advertising, trade press and contractor seminars, or influencer social media marketing. Which should QLC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television: TV would create rapid, wide awareness of low-carbon concrete among millions of viewers, which could help a public limited company build its brand. The trouble is that the buyers are the 500 contractors in QLC's research, not the general public, so most of the airtime is wasted. With $1,050,000 already committed to the plant, a national campaign is expensive and cannot convey the technical strength data contractors need before specifying.

Trade press and contractor seminars: These reach the 500 surveyed contractors directly, of whom 57% would specify low-carbon concrete and 49% accept a $0.80 premium. Seminars let QLC demonstrate the 2.1% pilot waste and 2.2% failed-batch performance, answer engineering questions and capture specifications. Costs are modest and measurable, though the audience is narrow and results depend on getting specifiers into the room.

Influencer social media: Influencers can generate cheap, engaging content and raise awareness of green construction quickly, which may support the 49% premium signal. But influencer audiences are largely consumer-oriented rather than the contractors who buy ready-mixed concrete, and the 4-day delivery cycle means awareness without specification does not create orders, so conversion would be weak.

Recommendation: QLC should choose trade press and contractor seminars. They target the exact 500 buyers, prove the technical and environmental case, and cost far less than television, rejected as costly and untargeted. Influencer marketing is rejected as consumer-focused and unlikely to convert into specifications for the $1,050,000 plant; QLC can use it as low-cost supporting content later.

Because QLC supplies ready-mixed concrete within a 4-day window, close contact with contractors also supports delivery reliability, not just the launch message, which helps defend the 57% specification interest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with little QLC context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to QLC's contractor market.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why television and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: QLC wants to cut the 4.5% offcut waste on its conventional line. Explain two benefits for QLC of introducing team working and a quality bonus.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the workforce of 75 share practical ideas for reducing the 4.5% offcut waste, pooling the experience of operators who see the batching process daily. Small changes suggested by the team helped the pilot reach 2.1% waste, and collective responsibility makes it easier to sustain the 2.2% failed-batch rate across the whole plant, protecting the $21.00 selling price.

Point 2: A quality bonus gives a direct financial incentive to cut waste and failed batches, aligning workers' pay with QLC's aim of lifting operating profit. Because the $12.00 variable cost is charged on every cubic metre, less waste means lower costs and a bigger contribution to cover the $450,000 fixed costs and the $400,000 bank loan. A bonus tied to the 2.1% pilot benchmark also makes the target visible and fair, though it must be simple to measure to avoid disputes.

If the bonus is tied to the 2.1% pilot benchmark, the 75 workers can see a fair target, which reduces the risk of the 4.5% offcut waste returning unnoticed on the conventional line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to QLC's waste, costs and bonus.

questions.question_text: QLC must certify 18 of its 75 plant staff on the geopolymer mixer. Consider on-the-job training or external courses at $820 each. Which should QLC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the mixer is tailored to QLC's own geopolymer binder and quality standards, involves no course fees and keeps all 18 staff productive, protecting output of 90,000 units and the improvement to a 2.2% failed-batch rate. The drawbacks are that experienced operators lose time coaching, bad habits may spread, and there is no independent certificate, which could matter when 57% of contractors say they would specify low-carbon concrete and may want proof of competence.

External courses: At $820 each for 18 staff the cost is 18 × $820 = $14,760, small against the $1,050,000 plant. A recognised qualification supports the 49% premium signal and brings outside expertise that could push the 2.1% pilot waste standard across the plant. However, 18 of 75 workers are away from the batching line during the course, cutting short-term capacity, and a generic syllabus may not cover QLC's exact mix settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: QLC should choose external courses for the 18 staff. The geopolymer process is specialised and the credibility of a formal certificate strengthens QLC's low-carbon concrete claim to the 500 surveyed contractors, making the $14,760 worthwhile despite lost capacity. On-the-job training is rejected as the main route because it offers no recognised credential and risks embedding the habits that produced 4.5% offcut waste; QLC should add brief on-site coaching to cover plant-specific settings.

The $14,760 is small compared with the $1,050,000 plant, so the lost capacity from 18 staff is a temporary cost of protecting the 57% specification interest and the $0.80 premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with little QLC application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to QLC's 18 staff and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the $14,760 computation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how QLC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($21.00 − $12.00) = $450,000 ÷ $9.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $21.00 − $12.00 = $9.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $9.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways QLC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units to show a margin of safety of 40,000 units, indicating how far contractor orders can fall before the $1,050,000 plant stops covering costs.
2. Use the $9.00 contribution per unit to test the $0.80 premium: accepting it raises contribution to $9.80, so managers can judge whether a smaller discount still covers the $450,000 fixed costs.
3. Check debt and equity plans: at 90,000 units QLC is well above break-even, so managers can test whether the $400,000 bank loan can be serviced if infrastructure output growth slows to 3.2%.
4. Monitor unit cost of $17.00 ($450,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $12.00) each quarter; a rise would signal the 4.5% offcut waste is returning and trigger corrective action on the batching line.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $9.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 40,000-unit margin of safety vs 90,000 output; $0.80 premium modelling against $450,000 fixed costs; servicing the $400,000 loan; and $17.00 unit-cost benchmarking to track 4.5% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate QLC's profitability. Has QLC's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue increased from $1,500,000 to $1,750,000 and cost of sales from $900,000 to $980,000, so gross profit rose from $600,000 to $770,000. Operating profit climbed from $180,000 to $280,000 while capital employed went from $1,200,000 to $1,400,000; interest payable was $20,000 then $26,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. Gross margin rose from 40.0% to 44.0%, reflecting better control of aggregate and cement costs as the 2.2% failed-batch rate falls. Operating margin improved from 12.0% to 16.0% because operating profit grew much faster than revenue, a sign of fixed-cost leverage as output approaches 90,000 units. Returns on capital increased from 15.0% to 20.0%, so the $1,050,000 batching plant is already adding value per dollar, even after the new loan and share issue. The risk is exposure to construction inflation of 5.8% and to infrastructure demand growing only 3.2%; if orders soften, the larger fixed base could quickly reduce these margins.

Conclusion: QLC's profitability has improved: gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together, showing the investment is beginning to pay. To protect the 44.0% gross margin and 20.0% return, QLC should secure long-term recycled aggregate supply and convert the 57% specification interest into firm contracts.

Cost of sales rose by only $80,000 on $250,000 of extra revenue, so the improvement in the 44.0% margin is genuine cost control rather than simple volume growth, and the $1,400,000 capital base has been used more productively.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates margins and returns for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for QLC of using recycled aggregate and a geopolymer binder in its low-carbon concrete.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Low-carbon concrete meets a clear demand: 57% of the 500 surveyed contractors would specify it and 49% accept a $0.80 premium, helping QLC defend its $9.00 contribution per unit while recycled aggregate and cement costs rise 10.2%. The pilot's 2.1% offcut waste, against 4.5% conventionally, also points to lower scrap cost and a stronger green brand for a public limited company.

Disadvantage: Recycled aggregate can vary in strength and the geopolymer binder may cost more than ordinary cement, pushing the $12.00 variable cost per unit higher. If the $0.80 premium is not realised across all 90,000 cubic metres, margins shrink; inconsistent feedstock could also lift the 2.2% failed-batch rate and delay the 4-day delivery promise to contractors.

QLC must also keep the 4-day delivery promise while recycled feedstock quality varies; otherwise the 49% premium interest could be lost and the $450,000 fixed costs spread over fewer cubic metres. The 57% figure gives a realistic route to recovering that higher cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using QLC's survey, costs and batch data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in recycled aggregate and cement costs will affect QLC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If QLC's $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the additional 0.75 percentage points cost 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is small against fixed costs of $450,000 and can be eliminated by fixing the rate. Higher rates may also cool the infrastructure output that grew only 3.2%, a secondary effect on demand rather than a direct large cost.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.50 an hour): With a workforce of 75, plant and delivery roles include hourly-paid work, so wage costs rise. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so an annual total would be invented; the defensible check is productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 75 staff = 1,200 units per worker. If that is maintained the rise is absorbable within the $9.00 contribution; if it falls, unit labour cost rises and erodes margin.

Recycled aggregate and cement costs (10.2%): These are core inputs to every cubic metre. Because the $12.00 variable cost is not decomposed, only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.2%, that adds 10.2% × $12.00 = $1.22 a unit (about $1.224), or roughly 90,000 × $1.224 = $110,160 a year. Even part of that would cut the $9.00 contribution that must cover $450,000 fixed costs and service the $1,050,000 plant, though the $0.80 premium helps offset it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in recycled aggregate and cement costs has the greatest impact. It touches every unit, directly reduces the contribution that justifies the batching plant, and cannot be removed by fixing an interest rate. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be absorbed while 1,200-units-per-worker productivity holds, so neither is as damaging.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited QLC application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on QLC's costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
